rv.q: ...two-and-a-half hour stage send-off to their beloved horror anthology is a twisted joy
It is so raucously entertaining that it fails to matter, and I only left excited by the possibility of what, when this and Inside No 9 is really over, they might do next.
This is as ram-jammed with ideas as anything on the London stage.
Another wildly clever, madly innovative and suddenly moving show from this inspired duo.

From its murderous prologue on – hands-down the most memorable mobile phone announcement ever made in a theatre – this live show is as twisty and unpredictable as the best of their episodes on the BBC.
Tonight, on stage, the spirit of Inside No 9 is alive and kicking.
Overall the sheer craft and audacity of the attempt is satisfying and even stirring.
And yet, their habit of not only pulling our legs, but also constantly pulling the rug from under our expectations does become slightly wearing.
The stage show is less high-voltage, partly because it has not mastered the telly’s zooming closeups, both naturalistic and startling.
It’s a show in need of a stronger sense of purpose and identity: it’s not quite funny, emotionally involving or frightening enough, even though it has flickers of all those elements.

This dark and often bloody comedy by Steve Pemberton and Reece Shearsmith inspired by their decade-long anthology TV series is a mix of the intelligent and the obvious – part smart reinvention and part lazy cash-in.
All I can say is that the supposedly grand twist at the end landed with all the force of a blancmange.
Their humour is warm, and embracing; the cleverness of their story-telling robust.

Shearsmith and Pemberton are on fine form charging it with sparky wattage, fully flexing their elastic range by embracing the kitschy costumes, set changes, and slapstick dynamics of comedy double acts.
It is both a blessing and a curse, because while the form allows Pemberton and Shearsmith to wander through the Inside No. 9 back catalogue, it prevents the stage show from finding a solid core.
Inside No 9 fans will get what they expect: some ingenious plotting, touches of grotesque grand guignol, dodgy humour, great character acting and knowing references from the TV show’s back catalogue.
The production is fabulous across the board, and I haven't got one slightly unsure word to say about it.

cn.t: Shearsmith and Pemberton's stage spin-off delights devoted fans with twisty, inventive horror-comedy, though some critics find it relies too heavily on recycled TV tropes. Most praise the duo's theatrical ingenuity, but a few dismiss it as an indulgent cash-in.
